title: Commutes Sentence of Tena M. Logan
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Tena M. Logan as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department lists Tena M. Logan among the January 19, 2021 commutation recipients. It records a 168-month sentence, five years of supervised release, and methamphetamine offenses in the Central District of Illinois. The list does not specify Logan's revised prison term or the grant's release conditions.
description_long: The Justice Department's commutations table identifies Tena M. Logan as a recipient on January 19, 2021. It places the case in the Central District of Illinois and describes a 168-month prison sentence, as amended in 2015, followed by five years of supervised release. The listed convictions concern conspiracy to manufacture, distribute, and possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine, as well as possession of that amount with intent to distribute. These details establish the case and the sentence before the grant. The accessible table does not provide Logan's commuted term, indicate whether the remaining prison sentence was reduced to time served, or clarify whether any release conditions changed. Those terms determine the direct effect of the action and cannot be inferred from the original sentence. A clemency warrant or court record would be needed to describe the outcome more fully. The entry therefore remains limited to the documented grant and underlying sentence rather than implying that the conviction itself was erased.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Tena M. Logan as part of a clemency list.

notes: The DOJ list confirms the recipient, prior sentence, and offenses; it does not state the substituted sentence or release terms.

title: Commutes Sentence of Blanca Maribel Virgen
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Blanca Maribel Virgen as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department lists Blanca Maribel Virgen among the recipients of a presidential commutation. Her Northern District of Texas case involved a 360-month prison sentence, five years of supervised release, and a $50,000 fine for methamphetamine conspiracy and maintaining drug-involved premises. The public listing does not specify the revised sentence.
description_long: The Justice Department's official commutations list records Blanca Maribel Virgen under the Northern District of Texas. It identifies a 2009 sentence of 360 months in prison, five years of supervised release, and a $50,000 fine for conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and maintaining drug-involved premises. The same page names Virgen as a recipient of a commutation granted by President Donald Trump. A commutation changes punishment attached to a conviction; unlike a pardon, it does not erase the conviction. The listed sentence is the term imposed before clemency, however, and the public table does not state what term Trump substituted, whether the prison portion was reduced to time served, or whether supervised release or the fine changed. It also gives no reason for selecting this case. Those limits matter when describing the result: the record establishes that clemency was granted, but not the practical conditions or rationale of the grant. The case details provide context for the action without resolving its ultimate effect on Virgen's sentence.

description_short: Trump threatened punitive tariffs on imports from Denmark, Norway, and Germany unless they dropped objections to his push to acquire Greenland.

title: DOJ Opens Civil Rights Probe into Alex Pretti Shooting
description_short: Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Civil Rights Division opened an investigation into the Jan. 24 shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents in Minneapolis.
description_medium: The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division opened a probe into Alex Pretti's Jan. 24 shooting by Border Patrol officers in Minneapolis. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said Pretti was shot multiple times as agents tried to arrest him while he recorded immigration officers. Blanche described the civil-rights inquiry as separate from the Department of Homeland Security's review; NPR reported that officials had announced no timetable.
description_long: The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division opened a probe into Alex Pretti's fatal shooting by federal agents in Minneapolis on Jan. 24, 2026. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said Border Patrol officers shot Pretti multiple times while trying to arrest him as he recorded immigration officers on his phone. Blanche said the federal civil-rights inquiry was separate from the Department of Homeland Security's shooting investigation. He described investigators as able to interview witnesses, examine documents, and issue subpoenas if needed. NPR reported that the Justice Department was investigating Pretti's death but not the earlier shooting death of Renee Macklin Good by federal agents in Minneapolis. Blanche did not give a timetable for the probe or commit to releasing body-camera footage. The announcement therefore established a federal civil-rights investigation, not a finding about whether the officers violated the law. The reported distinction between the two fatal encounters and the absence of a timeline left the scope and public record of the review unresolved at that point.

title: Global Reaction Mounts as Trump Issues New Tariff Threats
description_short: Reuters compiled reactions after Trump threatened new tariffs following the Supreme Court ruling, with EU and others demanding clarity.
description_medium: After the Supreme Court invalidated part of Trump's tariff program, he issued a new tariff threat and drew responses from trading partners. The supplied account says European Union officials and others sought clarity about what the threat would cover. That reaction would show how the court ruling left trade policy unsettled, but the linked Reuters report could not be retrieved and the AP link addresses a separate tariff announcement.
